# The many faces of Narasiṃha

No important name has only one face. **Narasiṃha** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *narasimha* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Narasiṃha
- **ASCII form:** narasimha
- **Meaning:** "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu"
- **Domain of influence:** Man-Lion Avatar
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** नरसिंह (Devanagari)
- **Live domain:** narasimha.com

## Overview

**Narasiṃha** (*narasimha*) — Man-Lion Avatar · The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Man-Lion Avatar". The name means "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu".

**Narasiṃha** belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is associated with man-lion avatar.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Narasiṃha** and serves its temple at [narasimha.com](https://punicodex.com/narasimha/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *narasimha* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **नरसिंह**. Etymologically it means "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu".

Sanskrit Narasiṃha, from nara 'man' + siṃha 'lion'; the man-lion avatāra of Viṣṇu who slew Hiraṇyakaśipu.

The ASCII form *narasimha* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Narasiṃha** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

## Mythology

The stories of **Narasiṃha** circulate within the Sanskrit corpus, where the figure embodies man-lion avatar.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Narasiṃha is attested in the canonical Sanskrit sources as a figure associated with man-lion avatar.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Narasiṃha** is the man-lion avatāra of Viṣṇu who destroys the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu. Appearing from a pillar at dusk, he uses claws rather than weapons to circumvent the demon's boons of invulnerability. The myth celebrates divine ingenuity and the protection of the devout child Prahlāda. The image of Narasiṃha bursting from the pillar became a favorite iconographic subject, representing the omnipresence of divine protection in places where violence is forbidden.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **narasimha.com**. Behind the scenes the DNS carries it in punycode form — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Narasiṃha; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Devanagari can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Narasiṃha**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *narasimha* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 9 characters, 8 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **n** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.
